image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Multi-series line chart** (time-series line chart)

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Single panel** chart
- **Multiple lines** overlaid in the same axes to compare categories
- Includes a **vertical reference line/annotation** marking the “Start of pandemic recession”
- No faceting, stacking, or small multiples

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / time (2015–2024) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage relative to February 2020 baseline | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Worker origin (Foreign-born, Native-born) | Categorical/nominal | Line color/hue; line identity; end labels |
| Start of pandemic recession | Temporal event | Vertical reference line position on x-axis; text annotation |

comments.raw_comment:
This graph does not surprise me. Where I live, the Bay Area, the population is nearly 50% foreign born in some Silicon Valley cities. I enjoy this but I take issue with the fact that there is a monetary incentive for university programs to prioritize foreign student dollars, who have higher tuition, creating an international pipeline that take seats away from American born students. Second, I have seen the HB1 visa spectacularly abused. Executives and managers routinely across the peninsula bring over people it turns out the know from the past - maybe a friend from university days in India and other countries. Everyone wants to pack their work environment with people they trust, and they have a collective narrative that many native born are less uneducated, which is actually false.
Musk so much as said that.
It is NEVER just about merit at these companies. It’s about power, allegiance etc etc. It is also a complete fallacy that American universities aren’t producing enough engineers (are you kidding me?) So look closely at the medium and high paying jobs in the coastal cities now, and who has them. It should be a subject of grave concern for immigrants themselves because they don’t want their American born and educated children passed over either in the future.  American companies and non profits should offer jobs to Americans with preference, and prove it or pay massive fines. Americans need to be hired first ESPECIALLY in any office based here on American soil.

Let’s take the main message from these data as foreign born
Workers are, over time, playing a larger role in the U.S (and most other “Western” countries).

The question this raises is why politicians can’t be honest with their electorate:

- we need them (our “domestic” population is growing sufficiently for the roles needed).

At the start of the pandemic (x: 2020) both workforces intercept (y: 100%). Soon after (x~2020.2), the decline is much greater for workforce foreign-born (less than 92%) than it is for native-born (about 96%).
In the economic recovery period (x-axis from about 2021.5 to about 2022.75), which corresponds with the global effort to distribute covid vaccines and to minimize lockdowns, there’s a steep increase in the foreign-born workforce (from y axis: 95 to 106).  That means that it went from (30x0.95 to 30x1.06, which corresponds to 3.3millions increase. But, the native-born workforce didn’t increase or declined for this period.

In South Florida, healthcare saw a significant influx of foreign-born workers.   Many had ties to immigrants that had lived in South Florida for decades. But others came from places that had low-immigration history to South Florida. 
Depending on the kind of job (industry), many of these workers were either working illegally (through agencies) or legally (with temporary permits). 
Among other issues (higher rents and overcrowding places), there is a traffic problem in South Florida cities. And, places like Miami, FL didn’t seem interested in incentivizing public transportation or building more infrastructure to make options more appealing. So, traffic congestion and long commutes have become just the norm to get to work (or anywhere at any time).

Headline: In the U.S., millions of jobs happened for foreign-born workers after the pandemic. But, how?

I am an educated, experienced, curious, and open minded citizen trained in educational theory and practice, working in a renowned institution that maintains the public’s trust. comments.raw_comment:
* 	What do you notice?

The y-axis is drawn out (92% to 110%) making changes seem more dramatic than they are.

The actual number of foreign-born workers in 2024 it is 32.7 million (30 million x 1.09). The number of native-born workers in 2024 has returned to 2020 levels of 134 million. There has been a slight increase in the number of foreign-born workers. Native-born workers are still 80% of the workforce (134 m/166.7 m). They were 82% in 2020 (134/164). There has been a slight increase in the number of foreign-born workers in the US since 2020. I don’t want to do the math to figure out the change from 2015. I shouldn’t have to work this hard to understand a graph.

* 		What do you wonder? 
Why the Times chose to use a misleading graph? By design it visually makes things that are not equivalent, equivalent. Notably, at 2020 both lines intersect but the actual number of native-born and foreign born workers are very different, 134 millions versus 30 million, respectively. 

How many readers will misinterpret this graph as being the number of workers in the workforce which then paints a more dramatic (but false) picture?

* 		How does this relate to you and your community?
This will inflame anti-immigrant sentiment by misleading the public and falls in line with the Republican agenda.

* 		Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

NYT Complies in Advance by Misleading the Public

Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "Who’s Driving the Post-Pandemic Employment Boom?" by Nathan of Libra Academy in Huntington Park, Calif.; “Foreign Workers on the Rise: A Post-Pandemic Comeback!” by Patrick of Aurora, Colo.; “Foreign-Born Workers Help Keep the Economy Growing” by Ron of Maine; “Life After the Pandemic: A Jump in Immigrant Labor” by Addison of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Convent Station, N.J.; “Employment Rebound: How Foreign-Born Workers Took the Lead” by Johan of Perth Amboy High School in N.J. and "Foreign-Born Workers Rebound After the Pandemic Recession." by Ms. Lasky AP Language Block 5, Middleton, Wisc.

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.

The next graph will be released by Friday, February 28.  The topic will be vaccinations.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston and Annie Fetter near Philadelphia, who loves to Notice and Wonder about all sorts of things (and hopes you do, too!).

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at the graph, I noticed that it compares the percentage of native-born and foreign-born workers between the years 2015 and 2014. In 2015, native-born workers made up 96% of the workforce, and foreign-born workers made up less than 96% of the workforce. These numbers gradually increased until 2020 when they both reached about 100%. After 2020,  when both dropped suddenly. Foreign-born workers dropped to 92% and native-born workers dropped to 96%. In 2024, Foreign-born workers reached 109% and native-born workers reached 100%.    
I wonder what causes the changes in the graph. I also wonder what types of jobs all of these people have. 
This relates to my community because during the pandemic many people lost their jobs and the number of people working decreased. 
A headline for the graph is “Covid Changes the Workforce”.

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the percentage difference between foreign-born and native-born workers in the United States between 2015 and 2024 along with the recession in 2020, due to the Covid Pandemic. Firstly, I noticed how at the starting year of the graph, 2015, native-born workers were at a higher percentage than foreign-born workers, but their percentage quickly rose. I also saw how native-born workers had a continuous percentage that did not plummet or skyrocket, unlike the foreign-born workers. In 2020, right after the beginning of the pandemic recession, the foreign-born workers’ percentages quickly plummeted. I wonder if this is because they could not travel at the height of the pandemic. I also noticed that foreign-born workers quickly skyrocketed again and if this can be related to President Biden opening up the border to people from other countries. I also wonder if future foreign policy will change these percentages by closing the border or deporting those from other countries. This relates to myself and the community because it shows that my community has workers from all over the world and how they work to afford the basic necessities of everyday life. A title could be: “Foreign-born vs. native-born: Who dominates the US?”

1. I notice that there has been more of an uprising in foreign-born workers, and that first there was a spike, then a really big drop until it increased again. Foreign-born workers increased so much that there are more of them than native-born workers. But, as soon as the start of the pandemic recession, there was about the same amounts of workers from both sides, but foreign-born workers had dropped a lot more than the native-workers for a bit.
2. I wonder why the foreign-born workers had dropped so much more compared to the native-born workers. Why did they have such a dramatic drop, but now are suddenly so much higher in the graph than the native-born workers? Why is the amount of native born workers mostly constant?
3. My community is full of foreign-born workers, as most are from Hispanic countries and are immigrants, coming to start new lives in the US. I do remember almost no one working or having a job in my town once the pandemic began, which is reflective on both the foreign-born workers and also the native-born workers. Now my town is full of hard workers again, with both immigrant workers, and the children of these immigrants born here.

comments.raw_comment:
Observations - This graph shows the % of workers above or below the Feb. 2020 baseline by their origin. From 2015 to 2020, the % of native born workers was relatively constant, while the % of foreign born workers steadily increased each year. However, after Feb 2020, both the %’s of native and foreign born workers dropped. Foreign Born workers % dropped significantly more than native born. Native Born %’s recovered relatively quickly, but foreign born %’s began increasing exponentially in from 2022 and onwards. 

Questions - I wonder what caused the percentage of foreign workers to increase so dramatically to the point it surpassed the % of native born workers. Why did native born workers not suffer as much of a decline as foreign-born, and how did they recover so fast? What industries were affected by these workforce changes and how does this impact the economy? 

Relation to Community - NJ has a diverse population and is home to many foreign-born residents. These trends could mark a shift in the local labor markets. Perhaps the sharp rise in foreign-born workers may signal new policy changes or labor shortages in certain industries.

Headline - "Who’s Filling the Jobs? Tracking the Shifts in Native and Foreign Labor"
